newsitem.title: USA: Judge backs tests on King assassination gun.
newsitem.headline: Judge backs tests on King assassination gun.

text.p: A judge on Thursday backed new tests on the rifle purportedly used to kill Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968, a move that could lead to a trial for the civil rights leader's convicted assassin.

The ruling pumped fresh energy into the conspiracy speculation that has dogged the tragedy for three decades. But it was problematic whether James Earl Ray -- who confessed to killing King and then denied it -- would ever get his day in court.
The 68-year-old Ray is gravely ill with liver disease that may kill him in a matter of weeks.
In addition Thursday's order, which itself will likely be challenged, was only a recommendation that a state appeals court take up the ballistics test issue.

The ruling by Judge Joseph Brown in Shelby County Criminal Court hinged on a new state law which states that closed cases may be re-opened if there is a reasonable possibility that new scientific tests can prove a person's innocence, the judge told reporters following his decision.
Ray's lawyers had argued that sophisticated new tests involving the use of an electron microscope could show that the rifle on which Ray's fingerprints were found was not the murder weapon.

But John Campbell, assistant district attorney for the county, told reporters that anyone who thinks Ray will ever come to trial is "hallucinating ... we know several of the witnesses are dead and 30 years later it would be difficult to present the evidence."

Because Ray pleaded guilty he avoided a trial and possible death sentence. He was sentenced to 99 years in jail, but changed his story almost immediately and said that a mysterious accomplice actually did the shooting.
King's widow and son both testified in favour of reopening the case on Thursday.
William Pepper, Ray's lead attorney, told the court that Ray "has always alleged that the rifle in evidence is not the murder weapon, but a throw-down gun."
A firearms testing expert testified that the bullet, now fragmented, was still "in good condition" for testing and "not deformed."

King's widow Coretta and son Dexter looked on as Pepper said: "In the 28-year history of this case, (Ray) has never had the right to test this rifle. The defence has never had the right to have access to FBI test fire worksheet reports nor House Select Committee test fire worksheet reports.
"What we are seeking here for the first time ... is an oppportunity to test this rifle in an effort to exclude it for all time as the murder weapon."

Coretta King later testified that a trial is "our last hope to reveal the truth about my husband's assassination." If Ray is denied a trial, she said, "our family and indeed the whole nation will be denied the due process of law."

The congressional panel concluded that Ray was the sole assassin. Pepper has said that he believed King was shot by someone hiding in a bush outside the rooming house and that the slaying was a plot that involved the Mafia.
Other conspiracy theorists have blamed the FBI and even the U.S. military.
Ray is in a Nashville jail and did not attend the hearing.
